claims.text: Phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is governed by a thermodynamically driven order-disorder transition.
The initial Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 alloy is a homogeneous, high-temperature disordered BCC phase.
Cooling causes energetically favorable Al ordering that triggers separation into an ordered B2 phase embedded in a disordered BCC matrix.
The controlled comparison is slow cooling versus rapid quenching from the same high-temperature state at constant composition.
Slow cooling permits equilibrium ordering, whereas rapid quenching freezes the high-temperature state.
The expected order-disorder transition occurs approximately within 1000–1200 K.
The experiments exclude external stresses and compositional gradients and use diffusion-favorable conditions.
The structural mediator is nucleation and growth of B2-ordered precipitates.
Preferential ordering of Al atoms within the BCC lattice mediates B2 precipitation.
A composition-dependent thermodynamic instability associated with the energetic benefit of Al ordering drives the BCC-to-B2 transformation.
Diffusion during slow cooling allows Al atoms to rearrange into an ordered B2 structure.
Rapid quenching retains a metastable disordered BCC structure.
Slow-cooled samples will have more B2 ordering than rapidly quenched samples, detectable by B2 superlattice peaks in XRD.
Electron microscopy will reveal ordered microstructural features in slow-cooled samples.
DSC will reveal an order-disorder thermal event within the expected transition window.
The as-cast alloy is an appropriate baseline representing the high-temperature disordered BCC phase.
Extremely high cooling rates can kinetically suppress B2 formation, while sufficiently equilibrating conditions can produce full equilibrium transformation.
The exact transition temperature and B2 phase fraction depend on subtle compositional variations and experimental parameters.
Failure of slow cooling to produce a statistically significant increase in B2 fraction relative to quenching, or absence of a DSC event in the expected window, falsifies the hypothesis.
